name: Fatima Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Fatima, 43, a junior electrician after changing from invoice work. I have a vocational certificate, still find complicated circuit drawings difficult, and work under a senior who checks and signs off installations. My pay is above the usual rate, my partner Sam works in a bakery, and we've two schoolchildren aged eleven and sixteen, a mortgage, and nine months of expenses saved. Plenty of electrical employers work nearby; I like seeing a neat row of fittings at the end of the day, use a paper notebook, never use AI, and get worn out when someone explains a new phone system as if everyone learns by tapping around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a quieter story sounds welcome. If a few letters get written faster, that's fine, but I still need a clear drawing and somebody to check my work. I'd rather learn one task properly than pretend a new screen makes me faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our bills and mortgage are covered by the regular wages, with nine months saved behind them. I'm well paid here even though I still need help, and there are other electrical firms nearby. I feel secure enough to learn at an honest pace instead of hiding what I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing supervised wiring shifts now and through the next year. This week I'd ask the senior to mark one confusing part of each drawing in my paper notebook during the ordinary paid shift. I'd keep the family budget as it is rather than buy a new device or course because of this modest change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and relieved at the thought of some ordinary weeks. I can be tired from learning without thinking the household is on a cliff edge. Having savings makes a difference to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use those marked notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd explain the marked bit back before starting the task, so the senior could catch what I'd still misunderstood. Then the actual installation would get the usual check. My notebook is a reminder, not an authority to work alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about a good day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sam about one thing I could do better than last month. My partner would ask if I'd remembered the school form, which brings the size of the day back down. I like having a life where work isn't the only problem on the table.

say: I'd welcome **quieter change** while learning electrical tasks properly.
I'd still need a **clear drawing** and supervision, whatever office letters become easier to write.
think: Regular wages cover essentials, and **nine months saved** makes the mortgage feel secure.
High pay and **nearby employers** give me room to admit what I still need to learn.
do: Keep **supervised wiring shifts** through the next year.
Ask the senior to mark **confusing drawings** in my notebook inside ordinary paid shifts.
feel: **Calm and relieved**, with household savings allowing ordinary tiredness without immediate financial fear.
S0.quote: My notebook is a reminder, not an authority to work alone.
fieldNote: Her **financial security** coexists with junior skill; high pay does not become a licence or independent sign-off authority.
She uses **paper explanations** within paid supervision and remains clear that reference notes never replace checking the real installation.

steps.text: Keep supervised wiring shifts and marked paper notes within paid work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say show us where the quicker booking helps and where it just moves the waiting. I'd keep my paper drawing even if the office changes its system. I don't need to be against the tool to ask for a day I can actually follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own paid hours and our household income look secure for now because the site work and bakery work are mostly physical. I'm uneasy about the way a quicker estimate can make a learner look slow. I'd want the senior to judge the actual task, not a time allowance that forgot the checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for printed job details and a written explanation of any changed time allowance. During the first year I'd keep doing supervised tasks and note on paper when checking took longer than the estimate allowed. I'd ask for a review after eight jobs rather than learn the AI system myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I don't expect to miss a mortgage payment because the booking software changes. I want time to understand a new routine before somebody calls my caution a fault. The money behind us means I can ask without panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go into your paper record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd record the task, the expected time and what the senior needed to check. If I was simply slow, I'd write that too. A fair record should help me improve, not excuse every delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm says every allowance has already been checked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the same comparison against actual jobs before agreeing a shorter allowance. If the evidence was good, I'd accept a changed paper instruction. Accepting a proven instruction doesn't mean I'm volunteering to operate AI.

say: I'd ask where **quicker booking** helps rather than assume every saved minute reaches the site.
I'd keep **paper drawings** and ask for a routine I can follow while the office changes.
think: Our **near-term income** looks secure because both household jobs remain mostly physical.
I'm uneasy about **learner comparisons** that ignore the time needed for proper checking.
do: Request **printed job details** and written explanations of changed allowances now.
Continue supervised tasks and record **checking time** on paper.
Review the records after **eight jobs**, without adopting AI myself.
feel: **Uneasy about fairness**, while expecting wages and the mortgage to remain secure in the near term.
S1.quote: A fair record should help me improve, not excuse every delay.
fieldNote: She links discomfort to **assessment fairness** rather than silently predicting a job loss inconsistent with her stated expectations.
Her willingness to accept **proven instructions** does not erase resistance to operating unfamiliar AI tools herself.

steps.text: Continue supervised work with paper records of estimated and actual checking time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues thinking work changes in 2028, with capable physical robots around 2031. I wouldn't call that three-year gap a promise that learners are safe. I'd ask how the firm planned to keep people earning while it decided what equipment to buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink once capable robots handle fitting work, and another electrical firm might face the same decision. Our reserve gives us time, but it doesn't tell me where the next wage comes from. I don't expect to be helpless; I do think I should stop treating a familiar job as permanent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd redirect our 100 monthly holiday contribution into emergency savings, keeping ordinary mortgage payments unchanged. In 2029 I'd apply for actual paid supervised maintenance vacancies, only accepting written pay and hours that covered the mortgage and essentials. I'd stay with my present supervised job until such an offer existed, rather than buy an unfamiliar course in a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with time to ask questions instead of a need to say yes to the first answer. I could imagine the savings falling while I waited for the job I knew to return. That's the bit I'd need to keep checking, not just the machine news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check about a maintenance vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the actual duties with what I can do under supervision. I wouldn't claim my certificate made me ready to work independently. I'd also ask what equipment the new employer really planned to use. Another address isn't a robot-proof trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep the household plan realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam and I would review the household account every month and check whether both wages still covered the basics. I'd book fee-free advice if either wage fell or we were unclear about the mortgage options. I wouldn't count any relief or replacement income before it was actually agreed.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking work** from capable physical robots around 2031.
I'd ask about **earning during preparation**, without treating the three-year gap as permanent safety.
think: My **hours could shrink**, and moving electrical firms wouldn't automatically remove the same risk.
Our **reserve buys time**, but cannot identify or guarantee the next wage.
do: Redirect **100 monthly** from holidays into emergency savings now.
Seek **2029 supervised vacancies** only with written pay and hours covering mortgage and essentials.
Retain current work until an offer exists, seeking **fee-free advice** if wages fall or mortgage options are unclear.
feel: **Anxious with choices**, watching the risk of savings disappearing while familiar work fails to return.
S2.quote: Another address isn't a robot-proof trade.
fieldNote: She identifies **personal hours risk** without claiming a certain total job loss or abandoning the value of strong savings.
Her **job-change conditions** include actual vacancies, paid supervision and essential-covering written terms; relief remains unassumed.

steps.text: Redirect the 100 monthly holiday contribution into emergency savings
Seek paid supervised vacancies in 2029 with written pay and hours covering mortgage and essentials
Seek fee-free advice if wages fall or mortgage options are unclear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives me time to improve at this work and compare real options. The thinking change is in 2031 and capable robots follow around 2034. I'd rather check a promise in those years than congratulate myself for having more warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wages and reserve look secure for the next few years, so I don't need to jump away from the current job. I'm uneasy about later fitting work and how slowly I learn a new routine. There is time to check another employer carefully while still improving under supervision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd redirect the holiday 100 into emergency savings for the next year, then review the amount with Sam. Now I'd ask my senior for a paid ten-minute drawing review each week within normal shifts, without counting it as approved yet. In 2032 I'd apply for actual paid supervised vacancies only on written pay and hours covering the mortgage and essentials, keeping my present wage until an acceptable offer existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can make a decision in stages. I can try to understand one more drawing before trying to choose the whole rest of my working life. That's more useful to me than a rush of expensive promises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the paid drawing review is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep asking for a clear explanation during the tasks the senior already supervises. I wouldn't add unpaid practice or pretend that a request had become a training programme. Electrical work still needs checking even when paid practice is refused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge another firm’s offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether advertised hours had actually been paid through a quiet period. I'd want supervision explained as well as the hourly rate. A bigger number on an advert wouldn't help if the available hours couldn't cover the mortgage.

say: I'd use **five years** to improve gradually and check real options rather than celebrate warning time alone.
I'd keep **2031 thinking work** distinct from capable physical robots following around 2034.
think: Our **near-term wages** and reserve look secure enough to keep learning in the current job.
I'm uneasy about **later fitting work** and the time I need to understand a different routine.
do: Save the holiday **100 monthly** for one year before reviewing the amount.
Request a **paid weekly review** inside normal shifts, retaining ordinary supervision if refused.
Seek **2032 supervised vacancies** only on written pay and hours covering mortgage and essentials.
feel: **Uneasy but unhurried**, able to improve one task and compare another employer without resigning first.
S3.quote: Electrical work still needs checking even when paid practice is refused.
fieldNote: The longer warning supports **secure near-term learning** rather than an assumed new qualification or an automatic safer career.
Any **weekly review** remains requested within paid shifts, and applications require paid supervision and written household affordability.

steps.text: Save the 100 holiday contribution monthly for one year before reviewing
Keep supervised shifts while requesting paid drawing reviews within normal hours
Seek paid supervised vacancies in 2032 with written pay and hours covering mortgage and essentials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years lets me keep working without treating each new machine story as a final warning. I'd still put an annual review in the diary. Paying attention is something I can do without buying a whole new identity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and household income feel secure over the next few years, and time to become steadier at this job looks useful. I'll be 53 in 2036, still needing earnings when capable robots arrive around 2039. I don't know my future job, but I don't need to turn that uncertainty into a reason to leave a good wage today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep supervised electrical shifts now and request paid drawing reviews inside normal hours. We'd save the holiday 100 for one year before reviewing real costs, both wages and actual vacancies annually. In 2037 I'd apply for posted paid supervised work only on written pay and hours covering the mortgage and essentials, keeping the present job unless an acceptable offer existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, with the later question kept on the page instead of in every conversation. I could still enjoy our children's school years. I'd rather let the long warning give us time than use it to make ten years feel short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you act before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the review forward if either wage weakened or the firm placed a real equipment order affecting staffing. I wouldn't wait for the year 2036 while a change was already in our payslips. The annual date is a reminder, not permission to ignore real news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about their school choices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask which subject they liked and what the actual next course required. I wouldn't tell them a machine forecast had already chosen their future. I still have to learn at 43; I can admit there will be more than one decision for them too.

say: I'd keep working through **ten years** without treating every machine story as a final warning.
I'd set an **annual review** rather than buy a new identity to prove I was preparing.
think: Our **near-term work** and income feel secure, with time to become steadier at the trade.
At **53 in 2036**, I'll still need later earnings without knowing exactly which job will provide them.
do: Continue **supervised shifts** and request paid drawing reviews within normal hours.
Save the holiday **100 monthly** for one year, then review actual costs, wages and vacancies annually.
Seek **2037 supervised work** only on written pay and hours covering mortgage and essentials, retaining current work without an acceptable offer.
feel: **Calm** about the near term, keeping later uncertainty visible without letting it consume family life.
S4.quote: I wouldn't wait for the year 2036 while a change was already in our payslips.
fieldNote: Her calm reflects **secure current earnings**, while age 53 never implies a pension or protection for later fitting work.
The **later job option** retains paid supervision and written affordability, and actual wage changes can bring the review forward.

steps.text: Keep supervised shifts while requesting paid reviews within normal hours
Save the 100 holiday contribution monthly for one year before reviewing
Seek paid supervised vacancies in 2037 with written pay and hours covering mortgage and essentials

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my physical fitting work could shrink around 2031 before I've checked many alternatives. Honest notice of hours, paid explanations within the job and actual supervised vacancies would help. My savings give me time to ask twice; they don't make the first answer true.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how much easier it is to say I don't understand when I know the mortgage is covered. That money matters, but the supervisor's patience matters too. I'd like to be judged on learning the task safely rather than sounding confident before I do.

headlineQuote: My savings give me time to ask twice; they don't make the first answer true.
portrait: At **43**, Fatima is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, higher pay, and nine months of household expenses saved.
She and **Sam**, her bakery-worker partner, have two school-age children and a mortgage, with plentiful nearby electrical employers.
She avoids **AI tools**, prefers marked paper drawings, and accepts proven instructions without pretending she learns unfamiliar systems quickly.
Strong finances support **calmer preparation**, while fast change threatens hours and new work still requires paid supervision and affordable terms.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before fitting hours could shrink around 2031, before she has checked many alternatives.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest hours notice**, paid explanations within the job and real supervised vacancies would help her compare options without hurried promises.
